hello.note: Also means 'how are you?'. Hi and hello are just as common; formal: magandang araw po (good day).

goodbye.note: Paalam can sound final. Day to day people say sige po, mauna na po ako (I'll go ahead) or bye.

please.note: Pakiusap is a real plea. For everyday requests add paki- to the verb (pakiabot po = please pass it).

thank_you.note: Very grateful: maraming salamat po. With friends and equals: salamat.

youre_welcome.note: Without po: walang anuman. Casual: wala 'yon (it's nothing) or walang problema.

yes.note: Opo is the respectful yes, for elders and strangers. With friends and equals: oo.

no.note: With friends and equals: hindi. For 'there isn't any / I don't have it' say wala po.

sorry.note: Sorry po is just as common. Formal: paumanhin po.

excuse_me.note: Rather formal. Many simply say excuse me po, or call a stranger ate (to a woman) / kuya (to a man).

how_are_you.note: Kayo is the polite 'you'. With a friend: kumusta ka?

im_fine.note: Casual: okay lang or ayos lang. Ask back with: kayo po? (and you?)

my_name_is.note: Also: ang pangalan ko po ay … . Si is the marker used before a person's name.

nice_to_meet_you.note: Formal. In casual speech many simply say nice to meet you po.

where_from.note: Taga- means 'from (a place)'; the answer uses it too.

im_from.note: Join the place to taga- with a hyphen: taga-Canada po ako.

speak_english.note: Most Filipinos know some English, and mixing both (Taglish) is completely normal.

speak_slowly.note: Shorter and very common: dahan-dahan lang po (slowly, please).

where.note: To ask where something or someone is right now, use nasaan: nasaan po ang …?

what.note: To ask someone to repeat politely: ano po? or just po?

where_bathroom.note: CR (comfort room, said see-ar) is the everyday word for a toilet. Banyo also works.

can_you_help.text: Puwede po ba ninyo akong tulungan?

what_time.note: Clock times use Spanish numbers: alas-dos (two o'clock), alas-singko (five o'clock).

what_means.text: Ano po ang ibig sabihin nito?

one.note: Before a noun it becomes isang: isang tiket (one ticket).

nine.note: In quick speech it often sounds like 'shyam'.

bread.note: Pandesal, the small breakfast roll, is the bread you will see everywhere.

im_hungry.note: Na adds 'already, by now'. To an elder: gutom na po ako.

bill_please.note: In restaurants you will also hear bill out po! or just bill po.

delicious.note: To describe food calmly: masarap po ito (this is tasty).

no_meat.text: Hindi po ako kumakain ng karne
no_meat.note: Karne may be taken as pork and beef only, so also mention manok (chicken) or isda (fish).

enjoy_meal.note: Literally 'let's eat'. Kain tayo! is also a friendly invitation, even to someone passing by.

stop_here.note: On a jeepney or bus, say para po! to get off.

airport.note: Used on signs and in formal Filipino; in everyday speech most people just say airport.

train_station.note: In Metro Manila people usually name the line: istasyon ng MRT / LRT.

want_to_go.note: To a driver, simply: sa … po.

is_it_far.note: On the way: malayo pa po ba? (is it much further?)

one_ticket.note: On jeepneys you pass your fare forward saying bayad po (here's my fare).

too_expensive.note: Naman makes it a gentle complaint. More literal: masyado pong mahal.

cheaper.text: Mayroon po ba kayong mas mura?
cheaper.note: In speech mayroon is usually meron. To haggle: wala na po bang tawad? (no discount?)

id_like_this.note: Literally 'I'll take this'. Pointing and saying ito po (this one) also works.

pay_card.text: Puwede po bang magbayad gamit ang card?
pay_card.note: Also: tumatanggap po ba kayo ng card? (do you take cards?)

cash.note: Filipinos use the English word. Keep barya (coins, small change) for jeepneys and small shops.

open.note: Stress the end: bu-KAS. Said BU-kas it means tomorrow. Many signs are simply in English.

today.note: In speech ngayon (now) alone often means today: ngayon ang alis ko (I leave today).

tomorrow.note: Stress the start: BU-kas. Said bu-KAS it means open. The day after tomorrow: sa makalawa.

later.note: Mamaya means later today. Mamaya na! = not now, later.

good_evening.note: Also said when leaving at night. Good afternoon: magandang hapon po.

good_night.note: Said at bedtime ('sleep soundly'). When leaving at night: magandang gabi po. Many just say good night.

see_you_later.note: Playful and casual: kita-kits! Until next time: hanggang sa muli.

wait_moment.note: Also: saglit lang po. Casual: teka lang (hold on).

help.note: Saklolo! is also understood but sounds old-fashioned.

call_police.note: The emergency number in the Philippines is 911.

dont_feel_well.note: For pain: masakit po ang ulo ko (my head hurts); swap in tiyan (stomach), ngipin (tooth).

pharmacy.note: Drugstore is just as common, especially on signs.

lost_phone.note: Cellphone (or cp, said see-pee) is the everyday word. If stolen: nanakaw po ang cellphone ko.

allergic.note: This is how most people say it. Formal: may alerhiya po ako sa … .

be_careful.note: Ingat! on its own is also a friendly 'take care' when parting.

no_problem.note: With friends: walang problema. Also very common: okay lang po (it's fine).

of_course.note: Often spelled syempre. As a reply to a request: oo naman / opo naman.

maybe.note: Baka also means 'maybe', leaning towards 'it might': baka umulan (it might rain).

dont_know.note: With friends: hindi ko alam. Casual ewan ko can sound curt.

i_like_it.note: In speech ito is often shortened: gusto ko 'to. Gusto also means 'want'.

dont_like_it.note: Blunter and very common: ayoko nito (ayoko = ayaw ko, I don't want).

im_tired.note: To an elder: pagod na po ako.

welcome.note: What hosts say at the door ('come in'). On signs and at events: maligayang pagdating!

congratulations.note: To a friend: binabati kita! Casual and very common: congrats!
